summary: Cape Verde is an island nation in the Atlantic off West Africa, a former Portuguese colony and relay station of the slave trade, independent in 1975, known for its stable democracy and morna music.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: When the Cape Verde Islands were discovered by the Portuguese between 1456 and 1462 they were uninhabited; in 1462 the Portuguese founded Ribeira Grande (today's Cidade Velha) on Santiago Island, Catholicism arrived at once, and in 1533 a diocese was established, one of the earliest Catholic dioceses in sub-Saharan Africa. Both the colonists and the West African slaves brought there were baptized as Catholics, so Catholicism became the main religion of Cape Verdeans.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population is about one in ten, mainly young city people and residents who once lived in Europe or the United States. Cape Verde has a large overseas emigrant population and frequent contact with countries such as Portugal and the United States, and has been influenced by Western secularization; together with the spread of education, this has led some people to stop taking part in religious activities.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism mainly includes the Church of the Nazarene, the Seventh-day Adventists and the Pentecostals. The Church of the Nazarene was brought back in the early 20th century by Cape Verdeans who had worked on whaling ships in Massachusetts in the United States, and is still the largest Protestant denomination in Cape Verde. In recent years Pentecostal churches that came from Brazil have also grown rapidly in the cities.

religion.background: Cape Verde was uninhabited before the Portuguese arrived; in 1462 the Portuguese began colonization and brought large numbers of West African slaves to the islands, making Cape Verde an important relay station of the Atlantic slave trade. Catholicism arrived with colonization and blended with local Creole culture, and religious festivals such as the feast of St. John became important popular celebrations. In the 19th–20th centuries many Cape Verdeans emigrated to the United States and brought back Protestant denominations such as the Church of the Nazarene. After independence in 1975 Cape Verde has been mainly Catholic, with freedom of religion guaranteed.

language.official: Portuguese is the official language, while Cape Verdean Creole is the everyday language of the whole population.

ranking.name: Cape Verdean Creole
ranking.description: Cape Verdean Creole (Kriolu) formed in the 15th–16th centuries through contact between Portuguese colonists and the West African slaves brought to the islands (mainly from present-day Guinea-Bissau and Senegal), and is one of the oldest Portuguese-based creoles. Because all Cape Verdeans use it as their everyday language, about 95% of the population have it as their mother tongue, and each island also has its own dialect, such as the Badiu dialect of Santiago and the dialect of São Vicente.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: Portuguese arrived with Portuguese colonization in 1462, was the language of administration and education in the colonial period, and remained the official language after independence in 1975. Government, law, schools and the media use Portuguese, but in daily life most people use Creole, so only about 5% have Portuguese as their mother tongue, forming a typical diglossic society.

language.history: Cape Verdean Creole formed from the end of the 15th century into the 16th century as a product of contact between Portuguese and West African languages (such as Mandinka and Wolof), and is one of the oldest surviving creoles. In the colonial period Portuguese was the only official and educational language, and Creole was regarded as 'incorrect Portuguese'. After independence in 1975, Creole gained more cultural recognition, and in 1998 the government introduced a unified writing system (ALUPEC). Today the government is working to make Creole an official language alongside Portuguese.

ranking.name: Cachupa
ranking.description: A thick stew simmered for a long time from corn kernels, beans, cassava and sweet potato with fish or pork and sausage, regarded as the national dish of Cape Verde.
ranking.history: The history of cachupa is closely tied to Cape Verde's dry climate; corn and beans are crops introduced from the Americas in the colonial period that can grow in the arid soil of the islands. The 'poor man's version' (cachupa pobre) has only corn and beans, while the 'rich version' (cachupa rica) adds various meats. Cachupa left over from the day before is stir-fried hot the next morning and served with a fried egg, called 'cachupa refogada', the most common breakfast of Cape Verdeans.

ranking.name: Pastel (fried pastry)
ranking.description: A dough made from corn flour or wheat flour is filled with tuna, onion and chili, folded into a half-moon and deep-fried, with a crisp shell.
ranking.history: Pastel derives from the Portuguese 'pastel', arrived in Cape Verde in the colonial period, and was adapted with local corn flour and seafood. The waters around Cape Verde are rich in tuna, and tuna filling is the most common version. It is the most popular snack on the streets and in the markets of Cape Verde and often appears at festivals, weddings and parties.

ranking.name: Canja de galinha (chicken rice soup)
ranking.description: A thick rice soup simmered from chicken and rice with onion, garlic and spices, mild and gentle in flavor, often given to the sick or to women after childbirth.
ranking.history: Canja de galinha derives from the traditional Portuguese dish 'canja', and the Portuguese carried this soup to Cape Verde, Brazil and elsewhere in the colonial period. In Cape Verde it is regarded as a restorative dish, often given to the sick, to women after childbirth, or eaten on cold nights. It also appears at festivals and family gatherings, a home flavor that Cape Verdeans remember from their homeland.

ranking.name: Feijoada (bean stew)
ranking.description: A thick stew simmered for a long time from beans with meats such as pork and sausage, savory in flavor, usually eaten with rice.
ranking.history: Cape Verde's bean stew shares its origin with the Portuguese and Brazilian 'feijoada', reflecting the culinary exchange of the Portuguese colonial empire on both sides of the Atlantic. Because Cape Verde's climate is dry, beans are a drought-tolerant protein source that can be stored for a long time. The dish often appears at weekend family meals and festivals and, together with cachupa, is a representative stew of Cape Verde.

ranking.name: Grogue
ranking.description: A strong spirit distilled from fermented sugarcane juice, with a high alcohol content and a sugarcane aroma, similar to rum, the traditional spirit of Cape Verde.
ranking.history: Sugarcane was introduced to Cape Verde at the end of the 15th century by Portuguese colonists, and the valleys of Santo Antão and Santiago are the main production areas. Traditionally, sugarcane is pressed in a wooden press (trapiche) driven by oxen or human power and then made into grogue in a copper still. It has an important place in Cape Verdean society and is often drunk at festivals, funerals and music gatherings, and is also used to make 'ponche' with honey added.
